title: The Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9–14)
hook: one prays about his own virtues; the other stands far off and asks only for mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday, a servant let off a debt he could never pay went straight out and grabbed a man by the throat over pocket change. Your line was pass the mercy on. Did a debt you were let off come back to you? Day thirty-two.

Two men walk up to the temple in Jerusalem to pray. The first is a Pharisee, one of the most respected religious men in town. He stands, and he prays about himself. God, thank you that I'm not like other people. Not a cheat, not a crook, not unfaithful. Not like that tax collector back there. I fast twice a week. I give a tenth of everything I get. The second man is the tax collector, and everyone knows how he makes his money. He won't come close. He stands far off, won't even lift his eyes, and beats his own chest. And he says one sentence. Jesus tells this story, and then says which of the two went home right with God. The crowd did not expect his answer.
screen: `TWO MEN GO UP TO PRAY.` → `ONE LISTS HIS VIRTUES.` → `ONE STANDS FAR OFF.`

segments.voice: First, be fair to the Pharisee, because the story only works if you are. Pharisees were respected teachers of their day, serious about God's law, and much of the Jewish tradition that came after them grew from their schools. This man isn't a fake. He fasts twice a week, far more than the law asks. He gives a tenth of everything. He's doing more than anyone required. And his prayer starts well, with thanks. Then it turns: "God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are." He's praying with one eye on God and one eye on the man at the back. The whole prayer is a comparison. Now the tax collector. Tax collectors worked the system for the Roman occupation, and people widely believed they skimmed off their neighbors. His prayer in the old King James is seven words: "God be merciful to me a sinner." No list. No comparison. Just the truth, said once. And Jesus says: "this man went down to his house justified rather than the other." Justified means made right. Luke tells us who the story was for: people who trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and looked down on everyone else. Not Pharisees. Anyone. Which sets a trap for every reader. The moment you think, thank God I'm not like that Pharisee, you've prayed his prayer. The tax collector's line has had a long life. In Orthodox churches, the Jesus Prayer grows from it: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner. Monks and grandmothers say it hundreds of times a day. Christians in every church hear the same thing in this story: an honest sentence is enough to bring.
screen: `A GOOD MAN, DOING MORE THAN ASKED` · `A PRAYER WITH ONE EYE ON THE NEIGHBOR` · `SEVEN WORDS AND NO LIST` · `A TRAP FOR EVERY READER` · then, large: `GOD BE MERCIFUL TO ME A SINNER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one completely honest sentence. Settle, and breathe. Let the day come up: what went well, what didn't, what you're carrying. Now drop the list. Drop the comparisons, the part of you that quietly ranks yourself against somebody else. Find one sentence that's simply true. If you pray, say it to God. If you don't, say it to the quiet. It might be: I'm tired. It might be: I got that wrong. It might be: thank you. Say it once, then sit with it. Nothing to add. The bell holds the time.
The Pharisee and the tax collector. Two prayers in one temple: one a list, one a single honest sentence. And the honest one went home justified.
screen: `THE PHARISEE AND THE TAX COLLECTOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: honesty is the whole prayer. Once today, when you catch yourself measuring against someone, stop, and say one true thing about yourself instead. Day thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray short, honest prayers in their own words, and in Orthodox churches many repeat the Jesus Prayer ("Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner"), which grows from the tax collector's plea.

options: the Pharisee: he kept the law, and more.

original.note: Greek: "be merciful." the heart of the tax collector's seven words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a bad Pharisee and a good sinner.
what it means: the prayer that compares, and the prayer that just tells the truth. the trap is thinking you're not the first man.
what a scholar hears: hilasthēti, be merciful, shares a root with hilastērion, the word for the mercy seat, the place of atonement.
